Flowers春篇，完結撒花。
説實話，比起其他作品打完立刻寫短評，我更想靜下來好好思考一件事——我到底想在《Flowers -Le volume sur printemps-》的完結短評裏寫什麽東西。
描繪青春的作品很多，描繪青春傷痛的作品也有很多。校園題材的作品更是數不勝數。
但是或許聖彗星蘭學院它真的不一樣。裏面關於宗教的部分我很喜歡，也很感興趣。
而且白羽蘇芳也是一名相當有個性的女主角。
其實從tag角度來看，這部作品怎麽都算是一部高危作品，足以讓雷達滴滴響——宗教，姛，三角，原生家庭，推理。
但從結果來講，除了推理差强人意，其他都還真就平穩落地。
文藝作品的局限性非常地抽象。我可以很輕易地寫一個彈指一揮間就能毀天滅地，眨眨眼就能穿梭於星系之間的角色。但是我很難寫出六歲的女童，十四歲的少女，十八歲的青春年華。
但是我認爲Flowers春篇做到了。她們真的寫出了十四歲少女應有的樣子。
少女的思考、少女的迷茫、少女的經歷，以及最重要的——少女的思想情感。
我在想這是怎麽做到的。但是我最後放棄了思考。
因爲我想靜下心來，等待油菜花開滿山野。
沒開也沒關係，山野已經很美麗了。
然後是劇情外的事情。
首先是關於推理的設計，只能説設計得很好，下次不要設計了。不同綫路之間給的信息也完全不一樣，這怎麽玩。加上只有相關性沒有絕對邏輯性的答案且一旦錯誤直接BE，真是看笑了。
關於系統本身，存檔很多，選項也很多。但是有跳轉選項的功能很好，而且QSL也有相當不錯。唯一問題是這個淡入淡出效果比我命都長。手裏的過場動畫開始取消。
然後是一共兩個角色，還鎖綫一個角色。建議是如果非要這樣就在一周目刪選項啊，不然莫名其妙打個BE出來誰受得了。
以及八重垣艾莉卡太可愛了，輪椅角色全對（CV：佐倉綾音）。
總結：好的青春，果然需要友誼，戀愛，與輕飄飄的書籍啊。
劇情：三星半過，四星未滿
系統：四星少
全結局難度：中
總結：好的青春作品，果然需要書籍，電影，還有最重要的不能加多了，一點點懷著過去思念的文青。

I originally began playing this game about eight years ago. I've always been a fan of the concept of visual novels, but I honestly hadn't played through very many at that time. This one seemed sweet, so I decided to give it a try.

This story centers on Suoh, a socially anxious girl with some trauma in her past, starting at a Catholic boarding school. Her level of social anxiety has kept her from ever forming friendships, and this school's system of pairing up girls to support each other is very attractive to her. Suoh gets paired with two other roommates and has to navigate friendships and potential relationships with them and the other girls at the school. It is a beautiful and sweet story. But...

My one major complaint is that it's just too hard to get the good ending(s) without a guide. The puzzles require you to know a lot about the Japanese names for flowers and their association with classic literature. And I feel like this story didn't need a "game over" just because you get to the end without enough points.

[spoiler]Suoh's mistake while playing the piano (after being traumatized) should not make someone decide not to be with her. That feels disingenuous to the rest of the story, and only serves for it to be "replayable", in my opinion.[/spoiler]

I eventually restarted the game, following a guide for every answer. It was a bit tedious playing through the whole story again, and I took frequent breaks to play other games, but I really wanted to give Suoh her happy ending. So, here, in spring, eight years later... I finally finished the good ending. Just to discover that...

[spoiler]...there isn't one? I knew that Flowers was a series, but I'd assumed the games were only vaguely related, self-contained stories. Turns out, this first story ends on a cliff-hanger. I am actually a fan of cliff-hangers. (What can I say? I'm also a writer.) But after the agonizing process I went through to complete this game a second time, a sad "true" ending was really not what I was expecting![/spoiler]

Still, I loved this story too much to not recommend it. I deeply resonate with Suoh, having suffered extreme social anxiety most of my life. Rarely have I found characters I could relate to this much. My advice is to buy the whole set of Flowers and just use a guide to get through from the start. I'm hoping to enjoy the rest of these games, but admittedly, I might need some time to recover from this one.

I'm recommending the entire series in this review. I recommend Flowers because I think it's a wonderful work of coming-of-age fiction capable of standing alongside its early modern and contemporary English-language influences. I'm very grateful that Innocent Grey could produce something like this out of pure passion. Shimizu Hatsumi's witty and precise prose, Sugina Miki's subdued and elegant artstyle, and MANYO's classical compositions all contributed to rekindling that magical feeling I felt reading at a young age. Shimizu Hatsumi's love for film and literature is obvious, and her writing is both charming and transgressive. I was reminded of my own love of the magical world of literature, so Flowers will remain in my heart as something really, truly special, and comfort media I will always return to.

Flowers is very evocative of coming-of-age classics, but especially girls' literature like [i]Anne of Green Gables[/i] and [i]Little Women[/i]. Little orphan and insecure beauty Shirahane Suoh attends Saint Angraecum Academy, an all-girls Catholic school, to discover new kinds of friendship as she grows through the seasons alongside her peers. She and new her friends investigate a series of unusual mysteries linked to the academy, and in doing so uncover a lot about themselves and their places in the world. There's plenty of sugary sweet romance along the way too.

It's a simple but transgressive premise, and like any excellent work, Flowers tells many stories from many angles. I like to look at Flowers through the lens of performance. The way that recitals are used for storytelling is brilliant, but there's also identity off the stage, whether as a "daughter," a "Christian," or even a "lesbian." Flowers is also about how to get the things we want by navigating the imaginary rules surrounding those identities. Flowers could also be read as commentary on literature due to the conflicts that arise from Suoh’s quirky and bookish personality, or even as commentary on the genre of yuri itself with Suoh failing to recognize boundaries with her accidental flirting or how the explicitly identified lesbianism causes conflict with the seemingly idealized setting. But Flowers is also about music, the soul, and second chances. Love really is at the core of the story, and though it is also a fairy tale, it is surprisingly grounded. This is helped by its gentle approach to various subject matter. Even the genuinely taboo is handled with a lot of sympathy and care.

Of course there's a great cast of characters. They're not just enjoyable on their own, but they do well to demonstrate the writer's skill. Suoh may be a wallflower, but she has her own subdued playfulness and sense of humor that provides a surprising amount of levity despite Suoh herself not being comic relief. Each character has her own arc of development, but they're also written to be a complete set. Beyond sharing thematic and plot parallels, the sense that one girl completes another fits naturally with the setting's partnership system. At the same time, characters are naturally contradictory, expressing honest insecurities and lying about their secrets. As a long series, they're all given plenty of time to blossom. I'm glad that girls I initially wrote-off as joke characters developed in heartfelt, unexpected, and yet still grounded ways. I'm especially fond of Yaegaki, who has become my favorite character in fiction, and Suoh, who ended up such a wonderful protagonist. She really does deserve to be the star of the show because her unique quirks and admirable bravery are at the heart of Flowers' themes. I came to love her like a sister and always rooted for her.

Shimizu's prose is extremely precise, but she doesn't shy away from flowery language or detailed expressions. Hemingway's "iceberg" is a very appropriate analogy for just how much character depth can be concealed under such straightforward writing. A single line can address so many plot threads at once. She's also really witty. I was surprised at how genuinely funny Flowers is, and how often I found myself laughing (everything surrounding Yaegaki is a riot). Flowers delivers a lot of emotionally intense scenes too. I found myself moved frequently, swooning at heroism and weeping at heartbreak. The translation does well to convey this (even if it really, really needed more QA work).

The presentation is absolutely gorgeous. Flowers is easily one of the prettiest visual novels to have ever been developed. The illustrations are outstanding, and the backgrounds are a visual feast of color. The use of classical music immediately establishes such a warm and inviting atmosphere, and the changes with the seasons are beautifully appropriate. The voice acting is similarly sublime.

Printemps tells a beautiful story and provides an important foundation for deep development in the next volumes. I absolutely adore Été. Automne is widely beloved, and Hiver provides a thematic and heartfelt conclusion built upon tons of subtleties and reading between the lines. Flowers as a whole is very tightly written.

I love the bonus content. It's a shame that the voice cast interviews aren't translated. They're great! Sakura Ayane (Yaegaki) is hilarious and Akeshima Yuuri (Rikka) gushing about yuri in her excited voice is really cute.

Speaking of which, I think Flowers is a great homage to the genre. Literary references are just as much references to the history of yuri itself as they are thematic to Flowers. There are so many references to historical points like the early days of women's education with books like [i]Little Women[/i], when women were segregated and educated by Christian missionaries to be proper wives. Depictions of friendship, sisterhood, and what it meant to be a proper woman would carry over from the Meiji era into the Taisho era, where S culture and its unique, often more explicitly romantic depictions of relationships between girls would develop into foundational literature like [i]Hanamonogatari[/i]. Flowers' Amitié system and extremely spiritually deep relationships are clear homages to S relationships, and the meaningful use the language of flowers is recalls the influence of Yoshiya Nobuko. There are also references to broader shoujo culture, which contemporary yuri descends directly from. It's obviously reminiscent of the utterly foundational [i]Maria Watches Over Us[/i], but it also evokes a lot of nostalgic post-WW2 keystones like [i]A Little Princess[/i], [i]The Secret Garden[/i], and of course, [i]Anne of Green Gables[/i]. Flowers is so witty and romantic, and it has so much bickering, that it could be confused with Jane Austen, translated in the same period. 

There are moments bordering on outright deconstruction despite the extremely traditional presentation. Saint Angraecum even eschews some mainstream obsessions with girls' academies and is as in history: an institution boxed in by patriarchal society, not guarded from it by high walls (though Flowers does not shy away from voyeuristic points of view, Innocent Grey’s name lol). I think that Flowers is great at showing the genre's cultural and literary influences. It also stands at the pinnacle of yuri on its own merits. It has pining after a devout Christian girl, it has gratuitous French, and of course it has crossdressing. Oh, and obviously there are lilies. Mayuri is right there! It's clear that people involved with Flowers are genuine fans of yuri and have paid it respect in a unique but familiar way.

My First Visual Novel Experience: Flowers -Printemps-
​Overall Impression: A Bittersweet Beginning
After spending 30 hours on my very first Visual Novel, I’m left with a mix of emptiness and so many unanswered questions. Flowers provided an incredible first experience, even though I struggled with unfamiliar vocabulary and the vast amount of references the game threw at me.

​The "Brutal" Puzzles:
I’ve heard that the puzzles are a weak point if you aren't good at deduction, and boy, did this game crush me! As someone not great at riddles, being asked about things I’ve never encountered was a real challenge.
​Example (The Number 17): I was so confused! I learned that in Italy, 17 is considered unlucky because the Roman numeral XVII can be rearranged to spell VIXI, which in Latin means "I have lived" (implying "my life is over"). It was a "head-scratching" moment for me, but looking back, it was actually very interesting to learn something so niche.

​Story & Characters:
The narrative does a great job exploring Suoh’s painful past and her journey to move on while developing relationships with her "Amitié." The game gives us choices on who to bond with, leading to 7 different endings. I hit 5 Bad Ends before finally clearing the last two!
​The Endings:
If I had to choose, I preferred Rikka’s ending. Mayuri’s ending felt far too tragic to be a "True End" for me. It’s a cliffhanger that really makes you want to jump straight into the sequel to find out why Mayuri left the school. I feel so sorry for Suoh! 🥹

​Final Thoughts:
This was a perfect first impression of the VN genre. My explanation might be a bit messy, but I’m so glad I discovered this game. Huge thanks to the person who recommended this to me—it truly meant a lot.

​See you in the next season!

I love this VN, but similar to what a lot of people have been saying, [i]it could have been better.[/i] My first and biggest issue with the game is the mystery. They don’t leave enough clues for you to make a good conclusion when it comes to choosing an answer. 

For example, when we were asked which country has the most Catholics, I immediately looked it up and found the answer to be either Brazil or the USA. However, the answer turned out to be Italy, which makes no sense considering Italy’s disadvantage due to its lesser population. Another example is Neri talking about 13 being an unlucky number. When the game presented me with choices, I naturally picked 13 as the unlucky number since Neri mentioned it. How the hell was I supposed to know that the answer was 17 all along when the game purposely misled me and didn't even leave hints that the answer might be 17 instead of 13? This was definitely a big writing mistake on their part, which is a letdown. 

My second issue is Suoh's character. Don't get me wrong, I love her and all, but she was too easy on Rikka!!! Rikka literally blackmailed her into a relationship and she just forgave her so easily. I can't even get mad over her for that because it's just Suoh being Suoh. Speaking of Suoh forgiving Rikka, I wish we saw the full detail of this happening instead of seeing it through Mayuri's POV since their conversation wasn't even clear at all. 

My third and last issue is Mayuri and Suoh's romance. I wish that there were more time for Mayuri and Suoh to have more interactions after Chapter 7 so we could see how Mayuri's feelings for Suoh bloomed. And when they did finally get together, we didn’t even get to truly enjoy the moment because of Mayuri’s abrupt departure. As a result, their romance feels very anticlimactic. I personally wanted more lovey-dovey moments between them, and being left with an ending that doesn’t give me that feels unsatisfying. 

Despite all these flaws, the good parts still completely won my heart. I loved the amount of literature references, the character interactions (especially between Suoh and Yuzuriha), the phenomenal art, and the overall plot. I'd totally recommend this VN if you don't mind the flaws I just stated above. It's still very good and really worth your money. Reading this made me feel like a bum though because it was all I have been doing since Christmas break, but I would do it over and over and over again. Once again, thank you for the wonderful journey, Flowers -Le volume sur printemps-. Till I see you next time. 💗

This is the very first entry into the Flowers saga, told from quite the shy and reserved schoolar, occuring during spring.
While one may think of ordinary public school, It's about a unique and very extraordinary type of school, at least to me and many others who don't have such experiences.
The entry introduces pretty much the entire cast that's gonna remain present even in the later entries, so skipping this one and heading for the other seasons is highly discouraged, as not only will that cause the reader to feel left behind, but even the developments of the characters' personalities stop making much of a sense.

While the novel gives off a fairly lightweight theme at first, it does dive quite deep and it's gonna be a tough cookie to go through, all the more difficult the more empathetic the reader is.
That said, there's no reason to not give this one a try as it truly is one of the exceptional novels out there with a unique and at times playful plot, as well as natural developments.
Nothing over here feels forced, everything's connected and it does make sense.

- In case there'd be the question, it does hint at the romantic elements and getting attached to each other, but that's the usual as even classmates do get somewhat closer to each other upon seein' each other at school ín day to day activities, right?

The novel is also fully voice acted with quite polished Japanese, making it easier to understand and the voice actings are so memorable that it won't even take long to know figure out who's talking before reading the text.. I've had it like that, at least..


So, yeah.
The entry is crucial to the Flowers sequels later on, and to many remains the best or one of the best, quite likely because the characters do feel so natural and relatable at times that it eases up the reading and makes it a bliss.


Now, what I haven't mentioned yet..-

The soundtrack is exceptionally peaceful.
The overwhelming majority are going to be instrumental tracks that are easy to listen to, later on all the more emotional the more the reader gets into the story.. It will fit at the scenes, the atmosphere will be greatly affected by them, that's for sure.
The artworks are also sorta unique.. While it's nothing as the modern novels' digital arts with tonsa lights and vibrant colors, everything does belong here where it is and where it shall remain.


Whether I'd recommend it. That's one of the parts you as reading this review might be looking for..
-> I'd most definitely recommend this novel to people who're looking for some relaxing experiences that are just perfect to burn through the time without having anything to worry about.
The soundtrack, along with some of the easily understood jokes that do appear in the text and overall atmosphere truly provides for very special experiences, and that is regardless of the reader's experiences with novels, I think..
..
However..
-> I wouldn't recommend the novel to readers who are looking for some action; To readers who are looking for some novel that's easily read through without getting into it, and just as easily going into another one. That this novel can't do and doesn't seem to be written this way.


Whenever I've taken my time to read through the novel, which was only once if I'm not mistaken.. I do recall getting quite emotional at it. There's that bit of me that expects or takes crying while reading through any of the Flowers saga as absolutely inevitable and to be expected. It is so well written.. Not long, not short, but at the perfect length!
But what I must mention is that the novel requires an additional font to fix some of the text mistakes that'd appear for those who don't have it.

That's it from me,

To preface, I liked Flowers 1, but it's still a mixed bag. The characters and art style are pretty and sweet. I think the protagonist is enjoyable and relatable as well, as someone who is also socially anxious. The Christian missionary school setting also feels pretty well done. However, I do feel some of the experience is soured by the complaints I'll list below.

Firstly, to put it bluntly, the mystery-solving segments suck. They don't do a proper job of providing the clues and evidence in the game itself, and they pretty much expect you to already know stuff about the subject yourself, like the names of flowers, or about the book Wuthering Heights. I would be surprised if someone got these without having to look them up. You get a bad ending if you answer one of the questions in a segment incorrectly, so it's annoying.

Secondly, the route/choice structure is very flawed. Basically, throughout the game, you're provided with two choices at a time that either give you points toward Mayuri's or Rikka's routes (the two romance options). The thing is, though, the story is structured around Mayuri's route. Not only is it the canon/true route, but you can't even do Rikka's route until you complete Mayuri's, and to add another strike against the game, you get a bad ending for doing the route for the girl you don't have enough points for. 

This makes it so that first-time players who happen to make more Rikka-choices than Mayuri-choices (aka me lol) get doomed for a bad ending (since again, you can *only* get Mayuri's route the first time you play). I did check out Rikka's ending after beating Mayuri's, and it's so brief it feels like an afterthought. It all makes me wonder why they even bothered with a choice format and didn't just make it entirely linear, because it's so clearly made with Mayuri in mind.

My last big issue with the game is that it's a "setup" game, as in it's more about setting up the story that the sequels are going to build on and continue, so by itself, it feels incomplete, which is especially made clear by the ending, and leaves a bit of a bad taste in my mouth. 

Despite all my issues with the game, I still enjoyed it, so I would recommend it if you like Yuri and don't mind slow-burn stories, provided that you get the sequels as well, because you're definitely expected to play them all for the full story, and also that you use a guide to make sure you're choosing Mayuri-choices to avoid the bad ending. It's a very mixed start, but the sequels are better received, so get the series on sale and try it out.
